elements.name: Unit of Work
elements.what: Maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates writing out the changes and resolving concurrency problems in one commit.
elements.problem: Writing objects back one at a time causes many small database calls, ordering problems, and inconsistent partial updates; changes must be tracked and flushed atomically.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Identity Map
elements.what: Keeps every object loaded from the database in a map keyed by identity so each record is materialized as exactly one in-memory object.
elements.problem: Loading the same row twice yields two objects whose updates conflict and whose comparisons lie; a per-session lookup table guarantees one object per identity and doubles as a read cache.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Lazy Load
elements.what: An object that does not contain all the data it needs but knows how to fetch the rest on first access (variants: lazy initialization, virtual proxy, value holder, ghost).
elements.problem: Eagerly loading a full object graph pulls in far more data than a use case needs; deferring the load until first use bounds cost while keeping the object's interface intact.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Repository
elements.what: Mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers using a collection-like interface for accessing and querying domain objects.
elements.problem: Domain code that speaks SQL or mapper APIs directly couples business logic to storage; an in-memory-collection illusion isolates query construction and enables substitution in tests.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)
elements.borderline: Sits at the domain/persistence seam and is sometimes treated as a layer element, but it is a class-level construct implementable inside one component; also a DDD tactical pattern (Evans 2003).

elements.name: Data Mapper
elements.what: A layer of mapper objects that moves data between in-memory objects and the database while keeping the two schemas independent of each other.
elements.problem: Rich domain objects and relational schemas evolve differently; putting the transfer logic in dedicated mappers lets neither side know about the other.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Active Record
elements.what: An object that wraps one row of a database table, encapsulating the database access and adding domain logic on that data.
elements.problem: For CRUD-shaped domains, separating data access from domain behavior adds indirection with little payoff; fusing row data, persistence methods, and logic in one class is the simplest thing that works.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Table Data Gateway
elements.what: An object that acts as the single gateway to a database table, with one instance handling all the rows and methods for the table's SQL.
elements.problem: Scattering SQL through application code makes schema change and testing painful; centralizing all queries for a table behind one stateless object confines the SQL to one place.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Row Data Gateway
elements.what: An object that acts as a gateway to a single database row, one instance per row, exposing the row's fields and its insert/update/delete operations.
elements.problem: Code that manipulates individual records needs record-shaped access without embedding SQL at every use site; a per-row gateway object gives record semantics while confining the database code.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Registry
elements.what: A well-known object that other objects use to find common objects and services, typically via static or thread-scoped accessors.
elements.problem: Some widely needed objects (connections, configuration, current session) cannot sensibly be threaded through every call chain; a known lookup point provides access while keeping scope (process, thread, session) explicit.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Value Object
elements.what: A small immutable object, such as a date or money amount, whose equality is based on its attribute values rather than on identity.
elements.problem: Treating conceptually value-like data as identity-bearing objects invites aliasing bugs and wrong equality; value semantics (immutability, whole-value replacement, structural equality) make such data safe to share and compare.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Money
elements.what: A value object representing a monetary amount together with its currency, with allocation/rounding rules that conserve the total.
elements.problem: Representing money as bare floats loses cents to rounding and silently mixes currencies; a dedicated type enforces currency safety and distributes remainders deterministically.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Special Case
elements.what: A subclass that provides special behavior for particular cases (missing customer, unknown value), returned in place of null or an error code.
elements.problem: Callers otherwise repeat the same null/edge-case checks everywhere; a polymorphic special-case object answers the common protocol with safe defaults, removing conditional clutter (Null Object is the best-known instance).
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Plugin
elements.what: Links classes to an abstraction during configuration rather than compilation, so behavior is selected per deployment via configuration.
elements.problem: Behavior that varies by environment (id generation, tax rules, test doubles) should not require recompiling or littering code with conditionals; a configuration-time linkage point centralizes the substitution.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Gateway
elements.what: An object that encapsulates access to an external system or resource behind an interface shaped for the application's needs.
elements.problem: External APIs are awkward, unstable, and hard to fake; wrapping them in a thin application-owned object keeps the awkwardness in one place and makes the boundary swappable for testing.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Mapper
elements.what: An object that sets up communication between two independent subsystems that must remain ignorant of each other.
elements.problem: Two subsystems need to exchange data without either taking a dependency on the other; a third-party object owned by neither performs the transfer and isolates the coupling.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Layer Supertype
elements.what: A common superclass for all types in a layer, holding the behavior every member of that layer shares.
elements.problem: Every domain object or every mapper repeats the same boilerplate (id handling, common hooks); hoisting it into one per-layer base class removes the duplication.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Separated Interface
elements.what: Defines an interface in a separate package from its implementation so clients depend only on the interface package.
elements.problem: A client package must call functionality whose implementation it should not depend on (to break cycles or invert a dependency); placing the interface with the client and the implementation elsewhere reverses the compile-time dependency.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Optimistic Offline Lock
elements.what: Prevents conflicts between concurrent business transactions by validating at commit time (typically via a version field) that no other session changed the data since it was read.
elements.problem: Business transactions span multiple requests and cannot hold database locks throughout; assuming conflict is rare, detect it at commit and roll back the loser instead of blocking everyone.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Pessimistic Offline Lock
elements.what: Prevents conflicts between concurrent business transactions by acquiring an application-managed lock on data before working with it, forcing other sessions to wait or be refused.
elements.problem: When conflicts are likely or losing work at commit is unacceptable, optimistic validation is too costly; an explicit lock table owned by the application serializes access across long-running sessions.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Coarse-Grained Lock
elements.what: Locks a group of related objects with a single lock (often a shared version object or a lock on an aggregate root) instead of locking each member.
elements.problem: Locking every object in a cluster is expensive and deadlock-prone when the cluster changes as a unit; one lock covering the whole group makes acquisition atomic and cheap.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Implicit Lock
elements.what: Has framework or layer-supertype code acquire the needed offline locks automatically so application code cannot forget them.
elements.problem: Offline locking only works if every code path locks correctly, and one forgotten lock silently corrupts data; moving acquisition into shared plumbing makes locking unskippable.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Query Object
elements.what: An object that represents a database query as a structure of criteria referring to domain classes, later translated into SQL.
elements.problem: Embedding SQL strings couples domain code to table schemas and duplicates query logic; building queries as interpretable objects lets them be composed, checked, and retargeted.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Embedded Value
elements.what: Maps a value object into the columns of its owner's table rather than giving it a table of its own.
elements.problem: Small value objects (money, date range) do not merit their own tables and joins; flattening their fields into the owning record keeps the object model rich and the schema simple.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Serialized LOB
elements.what: Persists an object graph by serializing it into a single large object (BLOB/CLOB) stored in one database field.
elements.problem: A hierarchic object cluster that is always read and written whole is painful to shred into relational rows; serializing the whole graph into one column trades queryability for simplicity.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)
elements.borderline: As much a persistence-encoding decision as an in-program mechanism, but the serialize/deserialize machinery is implemented inside one component.

elements.name: Metadata Mapping
elements.what: Holds the object-relational mapping details as metadata (tables/files or annotations) interpreted or code-generated at runtime, instead of hand-coding each mapper.
elements.problem: Dozens of hand-written mappers are repetitive and drift from the schema; expressing the mapping once as data lets generic code perform it uniformly.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)
elements.borderline: Shades toward ORM-framework architecture; included as the in-program metadata-interpretation mechanism.

elements.name: Data Transfer Object
elements.what: An object that carries data between processes or layers in a single package, with serialization support and no behavior beyond storage.
elements.problem: Chatty fine-grained remote or cross-layer calls are expensive; batching the needed data into one dumb, serializable object reduces round trips and decouples wire shape from domain shape.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Identity Field
elements.what: Saves the database identity (primary key) as a field in the in-memory object to maintain the correspondence between object and row.
elements.problem: Objects and rows must be matched reliably across loads and saves; storing the key in the object gives every domain object a durable identity handle.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Foreign Key Mapping
elements.what: Maps an object reference between objects to a foreign key column in the referring object's table.
elements.problem: In-memory pointers do not exist in relational storage; translating references to keys on save and keys back to references on load preserves the object graph.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Association Table Mapping
elements.what: Maps a many-to-many association to a separate table holding pairs of foreign keys into the two associated tables.
elements.problem: Relational schemas cannot store multivalued fields in a row; an intermediate link table represents the association that neither object's table can hold.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Dependent Mapping
elements.what: Has one class (the owner) perform the database mapping for a child class whose objects are accessed only through it.
elements.problem: Objects that exist only within one owner (line items in an order) do not need their own mapper, identity map, or independent updates; letting the owner map them simplifies the machinery.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Single Table Inheritance
elements.what: Maps all classes of an inheritance hierarchy to one table whose columns are the union of all fields, with a type discriminator column.
elements.problem: Relational databases have no inheritance; one wide table avoids joins and moves objects between subclasses cheaply, at the cost of nullable unused columns.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Class Table Inheritance
elements.what: Maps each class in an inheritance hierarchy to its own table holding only that class's fields, joined by shared primary key.
elements.problem: One-table-per-hierarchy wastes columns and one-table-per-concrete-class duplicates them; a table per class keeps the schema normalized at the cost of joins to assemble an object.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Concrete Table Inheritance
elements.what: Maps each concrete class in an inheritance hierarchy to its own table containing all its fields, inherited and declared.
elements.problem: Loading an object of a known concrete class should touch one table only; duplicating inherited columns per concrete table removes joins at the cost of schema duplication and cross-table key discipline.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Inheritance Mappers
elements.what: A structure of mapper classes mirroring an inheritance hierarchy, so each domain class has a mapper that handles its own fields and delegates inherited ones upward.
elements.problem: Mapping code for a class hierarchy duplicates superclass field handling in every concrete mapper; organizing the mappers as a parallel hierarchy factors the shared mapping once.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Service Stub
elements.what: Removes dependence on a problematic external service during testing by substituting an in-process stand-in that implements the same gateway interface.
elements.problem: Slow, unreliable, or unavailable external services stall development and make tests nondeterministic; a local fake behind the same interface keeps work and tests running.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Record Set
elements.what: An in-memory representation of tabular data that looks and acts like the result of a database query but can be built and manipulated disconnected from the database.
elements.problem: UI machinery and table-oriented logic want a generic table-shaped data structure independent of any live connection; a disconnected record set lets the same tooling work on queried or synthesized data.
elements.named_in: Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture - Martin Fowler (2002)

elements.name: Entity
elements.what: A domain object defined primarily by a thread of continuity and identity rather than by its attributes, with identity maintained across state changes and representations.
elements.problem: Some domain objects must be tracked through changes and matched across forms and stores; modeling them around an explicit identity (not attribute equality) prevents mismatches and aliasing errors.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software - Eric Evans (2003)

elements.name: Aggregate
elements.what: A cluster of associated objects treated as a single unit for data changes, with one root entity through which all external references and modifications must pass.
elements.problem: Invariants spanning several objects cannot be enforced if outside code mutates members freely; drawing a boundary with a single root gives a scope for consistency, locking, and atomic persistence.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software - Eric Evans (2003)

elements.name: Domain Service
elements.what: A stateless operation in the domain layer, defined by what it does rather than what it is, for domain logic that does not naturally belong to any entity or value object.
elements.problem: Forcing an operation that spans several domain objects into one of them distorts the model; a named stateless service keeps the operation in the ubiquitous language without inventing an artificial owner.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software - Eric Evans (2003)

elements.name: Domain Event
elements.what: A full-fledged domain object that represents something that happened in the domain, captured as an immutable record and used to trigger and decouple consequent behavior.
elements.problem: Side effects of a domain change otherwise get hard-wired into the code that makes the change; reifying the occurrence as an event decouples cause from consequences and creates an auditable history.
elements.named_in: Domain-Driven Design Reference - Eric Evans (2015)

elements.name: Fluent Interface
elements.what: An API designed so chained method calls read like flowing prose, building configuration or computation as an internal domain-specific language.
elements.problem: Constructing complex objects or requests through many setters is verbose and hides intent; designing return values for chaining makes multi-step construction readable and self-documenting.
elements.named_in: FluentInterface, martinfowler.com bliki - Martin Fowler & Eric Evans (2005)

elements.name: Collection Pipeline
elements.what: Organizes a computation as a sequence of operations (filter, map, reduce, and kin) each taking a collection from the previous stage and feeding one to the next.
elements.problem: Imperative loops with accumulating temporaries obscure the data transformation being performed; composing named collection operations expresses the transformation as a readable, refactorable pipeline.
elements.named_in: Collection Pipeline, martinfowler.com - Martin Fowler (2015)

elements.name: Specification
elements.what: Encapsulates a business rule as a separate predicate object that can test candidates for satisfaction and be combined with other specifications via and/or/not.
elements.problem: Selection, validation, and construction criteria otherwise get duplicated and buried in queries and conditionals; reifying the criterion as a combinable object lets one rule serve all three uses.
elements.named_in: Specifications - Eric Evans & Martin Fowler (1997)

elements.name: Event Sourcing
elements.what: Captures every change to application state as an immutable event in an append-only log, so current state is derived by replaying the events rather than stored destructively.
elements.problem: Update-in-place storage loses history, complicates audit, and makes past states unrecoverable; storing the events themselves makes state reconstruction, temporal queries, and replay-based recovery possible.
elements.named_in: Event Sourcing, martinfowler.com (Further Enterprise Application Architecture development) - Martin Fowler (2005)
elements.borderline: The in-component append-log persistence mechanism is IN; the system-wide event-sourced architecture style is parked for Phase 3.

elements.name: Quantity
elements.what: A value type pairing a number with its unit of measure, with arithmetic and comparisons that respect unit compatibility and conversion.
elements.problem: Bare numbers lose their units, inviting silent unit-mismatch bugs (feet vs meters, dollars vs euros); carrying the unit in the type makes mismatched arithmetic impossible or explicit.
elements.named_in: Analysis Patterns: Reusable Object Models - Martin Fowler (1996)
elements.borderline: Analysis-pattern (domain-modeling) altitude, but a directly implementable value type recurring across codebases.

elements.name: Range
elements.what: A value object representing an interval by its start and end (with open/closed ends), answering inclusion, overlap, and abutment queries.
elements.problem: Pairs of loose start/end fields breed off-by-one and boundary-convention bugs repeated at every comparison; one range type centralizes the boundary logic.
elements.named_in: Analysis Patterns: Reusable Object Models - Martin Fowler (1996)
elements.borderline: Analysis-pattern (domain-modeling) altitude, but a directly implementable value type recurring across codebases.

parked_architecture.name: Model View Controller
parked_architecture.why: Whole-app UI structure splitting an application into model, view, and controller responsibilities - app-structure altitude (PoEAA web presentation family).

parked_architecture.name: Front Controller
parked_architecture.why: Single handler consolidating all request handling for a web application - app-structure altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Page Controller
parked_architecture.why: Per-page request-handling structure for a web application - app-structure altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Template View
parked_architecture.why: Web-presentation rendering structure (markup with embedded markers) - app-structure altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Transform View
parked_architecture.why: Web-presentation rendering structure (transform domain data element by element into HTML) - app-structure altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Two Step View
parked_architecture.why: Two-stage page-rendering structure (logical page then formatting) - app-structure altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Application Controller
parked_architecture.why: Centralized point for application flow/navigation control - app-structure altitude.

parked_architecture.name: Transaction Script
parked_architecture.why: Way of organizing all domain logic as procedures per request - domain-logic organization, app-structure altitude (PoEAA).

parked_architecture.name: Domain Model
parked_architecture.why: Way of organizing domain logic as an interconnected object model - domain-logic organization, app-structure altitude (PoEAA).

parked_architecture.name: Table Module
parked_architecture.why: Way of organizing domain logic with one class per table - domain-logic organization, app-structure altitude (PoEAA).

parked_architecture.name: Service Layer
parked_architecture.why: Layer defining an application's boundary of available operations - explicitly a layer construct, architecture altitude (PoEAA).

parked_architecture.name: Remote Facade
parked_architecture.why: Coarse-grained facade over fine-grained objects to serve remote calls - primarily about distribution-boundary structure (PoEAA).

parked_architecture.name: Client Session State
parked_architecture.why: System-level decision to hold session state on the client - state-placement across tiers (PoEAA).

parked_architecture.name: Server Session State
parked_architecture.why: System-level decision to hold session state in server memory - state-placement across tiers (PoEAA).

parked_architecture.name: Database Session State
parked_architecture.why: System-level decision to hold session state in the database - state-placement across tiers (PoEAA).

parked_architecture.name: Bounded Context
parked_architecture.why: Strategic DDD: explicit boundary within which a model applies - system-decomposition altitude (Evans 2003).

parked_architecture.name: Context Map
parked_architecture.why: Strategic DDD: map of bounded contexts and their relationships - system-level structure (Evans 2003).

parked_architecture.name: Anti-corruption Layer
parked_architecture.why: Strategic DDD: isolating translation layer between two systems' models - inter-system boundary structure (Evans 2003).

parked_architecture.name: CQRS
parked_architecture.why: Command Query Responsibility Segregation - splitting a system's read and write models is an architecture style (Fowler bliki 2011; Greg Young).

parked_architecture.name: Event Sourcing (architecture style)
parked_architecture.why: The system-wide event-sourced-system style (event store as backbone, projections, replay across services) - the in-component persistence mechanism is cataloged as element event-sourcing.

excluded_notable.name: Ubiquitous Language
excluded_notable.why: DDD practice/communication discipline, not an implementable mechanism - process/practice territory (pass 7).

excluded_notable.name: Factory (DDD)
excluded_notable.why: Evans defers to GoF factory patterns; canonical naming and cataloging belongs to the GoF scout (dedup).

excluded_notable.name: Intention-Revealing Interface / Side-Effect-Free Function / Assertion (DDD supple design)
excluded_notable.why: Design principles/heuristics from Evans 2003 ch.10, not named recurring mechanisms.

excluded_notable.name: Smart UI
excluded_notable.why: Named by Evans 2003 as an anti-pattern / whole-app structure alternative, not a design element.

excluded_notable.name: Identity Map vs cache distinction note
excluded_notable.why: Not an element - PoEAA distinguishes Identity Map from a general cache; general caching elements belong to other scouts.

notes: Coverage: full PoEAA catalog triaged from the live eaaCatalog index (all 51 pattern names loaded this session, hence 'spot-checked' on PoEAA entries). Charter subset included plus altitude-passing entries the charter omitted: Data Transfer Object, Implicit Lock, Identity Field, Foreign Key Mapping, Association Table Mapping, Dependent Mapping, Single/Class/Concrete Table Inheritance, Inheritance Mappers, Service Stub, Record Set - all pass the altitude test (in-component ORM/testing/data mechanisms). Value Object and Repository are shared PoEAA/DDD names - cataloged once with ddd tag (dedup with any DDD-only sweep). Domain Event is named in Evans's DDD Reference (2015), not the 2003 book - popularized by Vernon's Implementing DDD (2013). Service Stub uses proposed:testing kind - no testing axis exists in the given list; the xUnit Test Patterns family (Meszaros: Test Double, Mock, Fake, Spy) is uncovered by any charter I know of and would dedup with Service Stub. Other thin spots: Service Locator and Dependency Injection (Fowler's 2004 IoC article names both; DI may be covered by a construction-api scout - flagging in case not); Notification and Presentation Model / Passive View / Supervising Controller (Fowler's further-development patterns) were left out - the presentation ones are parked-family kin, Notification (error collecting parameter) is a real borderline candidate no one may own. Money allocation and Quantity/Range confirmed from Analysis Patterns familiarity (established, not live-loaded).
